name: Jackson §15.2: braking radiation
description: Jackson §15.2: a charge that is stopped abruptly radiates a flash of every frequency (bremsstrahlung, braking radiation). This target stops the particle at once. The flash goes mostly forward, but not straight ahead: seen at an angle $\theta$ to the particle's last velocity it is $\propto \sin^2\theta/(1 - \beta\cos\theta)^2$, zero along the velocity and largest at $\cos\theta = \beta$ (here about 20°). The receiver straight ahead counts the band 100–200 and wants at least 0.005 per steradian: fired straight into the target the particle lights it not at all.

reality.represents: Bremsstrahlung: the flash of a sudden stop (Jackson §15.2)

remarks.line: Zero straight ahead, peaked at cos θ = β
remarks.detail: A stopped charge radiates as sin²θ/(1 − β cos θ)², every frequency alike, as Jackson derives.

Real bremsstrahlung comes from deflections by nuclei, over a short but finite time, so the spectrum is flat only below the inverse of that time; and in quantum theory no photon carries more than the particle's kinetic energy.

remarks.line: The radiation is exact for the motion
remarks.detail: What the receiver collects is computed from the particle's computed path with the exact far-zone fields (Liénard; the spectrum from Jackson's radiation integral), and the particle feels its radiation's reaction (Landau–Lifshitz).
The receiver averages over directions in the plane of the motion; the real radiation also goes out of the plane, where its pattern differs.
